title: Do You Have a Volume Problem or a Process Problem?
summary: Do You Have a Volume Problem or a Process Problem? - Explore insights, news, and resources from Intellinetics on document management, workflow automation,…
body_markdown:
When documents start piling up and work slows down, the instinct is to ask, "What should we buy to fix this?" It is the wrong first question. The better one is quieter and a lot more useful: what kind of problem do we have?


Get that right, and the fix becomes obvious. Get it wrong, and you end up in one of two familiar traps. You buy software to solve what was really a backlog, and now you own a platform and still must do the work. Or you throw people at a bottleneck that comes back every single week, because the process itself was never fixed. Software and services are not rivals here. They solve different problems. The trick is knowing which problem is in front of you.


**Two problems that look identical from the inside**


When you are underwater, every document problem feels the same. Step back, and almost all of them are one of two things.


A volume problem is a backlog. A decade of boxes in a storage room. A seasonal flood of enrollment forms. A cabinet of microfilm nobody can read anymore. It is a finite mountain of work that needs to get done once, and it is currently sitting on top of your team.


A process problem is a bottleneck. The same thing gets stuck in the same place over and over. Invoices wait days for approval. Records requests bounce between departments. Forms get rekeyed by hand every time. It is not a pile; it is a pattern, and it repeats no matter how many times you dig out.


They feel the same at 4:45 on a Friday. They are not, and they want opposite fixes.


**Volume problems want services**


A backlog is work, not workflow. That distinction matters, because software does not clear a backlog. It just gives you a place to put things once someone has done the scanning, indexing, and quality control. Buy a platform to solve a ten-year box mountain, and you have added a software project on top of the manual labor you already had.


Volume is what services are built for.[Document scanning](https://www.intellinetics.com/solutions/scanning) turns the paper and film into clean digital records, including the awkward formats a desktop scanner cannot handle.[Business process outsourcing](https://intellinetics.com/solutions/process-outsourcing) takes the whole intake-and-capture job off your team's plate, which is exactly what you want during a staffing gap, a seasonal spike, or a one-time conversion. A team that does this at scale clears in weeks what would take your staff a year of nights and weekends.


One caution on backlogs: clearing does not mean discarding. A lot of what is in those boxes must be kept, sometimes for years. The[IRS guidance on business recordkeeping](https://www.irs.gov/newsroom/taking-care-of-business-recordkeeping-for-small-businesses) is a good reminder that financial and tax records carry retention obligations, and other record types have their own. Clearing a backlog the right way means digitizing and retaining what must be kept, not just making the pile smaller.


**Process problems want software**


Now the other case. If the same task gets stuck in the same spot every week, more hands will not save you. You can hire a faster person to route invoices by hand, and the invoices will still pile up the moment they are out sick. The process itself is the problem, and software is what changes it permanently.


This is where automation earns its keep.[Intelligent document processing and AP automation](https://intellinetics.com/solutions/intelligent-document-processing) capture information from a document, classify it, and route it for approval without anyone rekeying a thing. The invoice that used to sit for three days moves the same day. The difference between this and outsourcing is important: you are not handing out the work; you are eliminating the manual step that kept creating the work. That is what makes it stick.


The test is simple. If doing the task faster would solve it, you may just need more capacity for a while. If doing it faster would only delay the next jam, you have a process problem, and no amount of effort fixes a broken process. Only a better process does.


**Most organizations have both, and that is the real answer**


Here is the part that makes "software or services" the wrong question entirely. Most organizations do not have one problem or the other. They have both at the same time. There is a backlog sitting in the file room, and there is a daily process that keeps generating a new one.


Solve only the backlog, and the mountain rebuilds itself, because the process that created it never changed. Solve only the process, and you have a clean workflow running on top of a decade of paper nobody can find. The two fixes are not competitors; they are a sequence. Services get you to a clean starting line. Software keeps you there. Run them together, and the backlog clears for good instead of coming back next year with interest.


That is also why the "just buy software" reflex and the "just outsource it" reflex both disappoint. Each solves half the problem and leaves the other half to quietly undo the work.


**A quick way to tell which you are dealing with**


You do not need a consultant to diagnose this. Three questions get you most of the way there.


Is it finite or recurring? A one-time cleanup points to services. Everyday friction points to software.


Would more hands fix it, or would it just come back? If more capacity makes it go away, it is volume. If it would return the moment the extra help leaves, it is process.


Is the pain in the pile or in the handoff? A pile of documents is a volume problem. A document that keeps getting stuck moving from one person to the next is a process problem.


Most teams, honestly answering these, find they are nodding at both columns. That is normal, and it is good information, because it tells you the fix is not one thing.


**Match the fix to the problem**


The goal was never to pick a side between software and services. It is to stop treating a volume problem like a process problem, or a process problem like a volume problem, because that mismatch is what wastes budgets and burns out teams.


If you are not sure which one you are staring at, that is a genuinely useful conversation to have before you spend a dollar. You can see[how other organizations sorted out their own mix](https://www.intellinetics.com/case-studies/) of cleanup and automation, and what the right combination looked like for them.
